title: Liquid Penetrant Testing for Oilfield Equipment | PT, US
description: On-site liquid penetrant testing for US oilfield equipment: wellhead overlay, stainless piping, alloy castings and skid welds. Mobilized to your site. Get a quote.
h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing for Oilfield Equipment: Wellheads, Alloys and Castings
html:
Atlantis NDT performs liquid penetrant testing on United States onshore oilfield equipment where a surface-breaking crack or leak path must be found on non-magnetic or awkward parts: wellhead and tree components with corrosion-resistant overlay, stainless and duplex process piping, chemical injection tubing, valve and pump castings, aluminum and bronze hardware, and weld repairs on skids and vessels. Technicians are mobilized to your yard, shop or lease with field materials suited to the temperature. Send the parts list, material and specification, and request a PT inspection quote.

Where penetrant testing fits in the oilfield

Much upstream equipment is carbon or low-alloy steel, and for that steel magnetic particle testing for oilfield equipment is the quicker and more sensitive answer. But wells produce fluids that destroy ordinary steel: carbon dioxide, hydrogen sulfide, chlorides and brine. Designers answer with stainless steels, duplex grades, nickel alloys and overlays, none of which respond to magnetic fields. Penetrant testing is the surface method that works on all of them. It shows any crack, lap, porosity or seam that is open to the surface, on any non-porous material, regardless of shape.

Penetrant has limits too. It does not see below the surface, it does not measure wall thickness and it is affected by surface condition. For wall readings and internal flaws, see ultrasonic testing for oilfield equipment.

The standards and the regulators

Wellhead and tree equipment is built to API Specification 6A, which sets requirements for materials, welding and surface examination, including weld overlay in ring grooves and sealing surfaces. Drilling and well-servicing equipment follows API Specification 7K and API Recommended Practice 4G for structures, with API RP 8B for hoisting equipment. Production vessels are built to ASME Section VIII and production tanks to API 12F or 12D. The penetrant method follows ASME Section V, Article 6 and ASTM E165, described in our Article 6 penetrant guide.

State agencies such as the Texas Railroad Commission, the Oklahoma Corporation Commission, CalGEM and the Colorado Energy and Carbon Management Commission regulate wells and sites, but they do not write NDT procedures; the standards above and the customer’s program do. Where a customer specifies a proprietary standard such as DS-1, we follow that document. Technicians work under the company written practice built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, and an ASNT Level III approves procedures and reviews reports.

What we examine

  • Wellhead and tree components. Corrosion-resistant weld overlay in ring grooves, sealing surfaces and bores; weld repairs on bodies and flanges.
  • Stainless and duplex process piping. Welds on separators, dehydration units, injection manifolds and produced-water lines.
  • Chemical injection and instrument tubing. Small-bore welds and fittings that carry inhibitors, methanol or glycol.
  • Valve, pump and compressor castings. Surface porosity, shrinkage and cracks on machined faces and weld ends.
  • Non-ferrous hardware. Aluminum and bronze housings and bearings, lifting fixtures made of non-magnetic alloys.
  • Weld repairs on carbon steel where geometry prevents a magnetic yoke, such as fillet roots on skid piping, socket welds and thread roots on small connections.

Technique and why surface preparation decides the result

A penetrant system works by capillary action: dye-bearing liquid enters a crack, excess is removed from the surface, and a developer draws the trapped liquid back out so it can be seen. If the opening is blocked, nothing enters. Oilfield parts block openings in familiar ways: hardened sludge and wax, paint, thread compound, scale, and metal smeared closed by wire brushing or blasting. We start by degreasing with approved solvents and, on soft or smearable alloys, ask for a light mechanical finish followed by chemical cleaning where the procedure requires it. After cleaning the surface must be dry, because trapped solvent or water prevents the penetrant from entering.

In the field we typically use solvent-removable visible-dye penetrant with non-aqueous developer, which is portable and needs no water. Fluorescent systems are used for highest sensitivity when a dark area is available, such as for machined overlay surfaces. Dwell is set by the penetrant maker and the code, usually five to thirty minutes. The usual temperature window for the test surface is roughly 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit unless the procedure is qualified for a different range, so winter lease work needs heated enclosures and summer sun needs shade to prevent the solvent from drying out during dwell.

Stainless and nickel alloys call for low-chlorine, low-sulfur penetrant materials, because residue can attack the metal. We use certified products, record lot numbers and remove residues after the test. Carbon-steel tools and brushes are kept away from stainless surfaces so iron is not embedded.

Overlays, ring grooves and sealing surfaces

Corrosion-resistant overlay is a thin layer of nickel alloy or stainless steel welded onto the sealing surfaces of wellhead bodies and flanges. It is deposited so the metal that touches fluid is corrosion resistant while the body stays strong and economical. Cracks in overlay are surface-breaking by nature and sit at the fusion line, so penetrant testing is the logical examination. Ring grooves are examined with the part cleaned, the groove free of anti-seize and the lighting adequate for a narrow, deep geometry. Our examiners look for cracks across the groove faces and at the base, and for porosity that could open a leak path under pressure.

We report what we find and where; the equipment owner decides whether to rework, repair or retire the part. Any repair welding follows the owner’s qualified procedure, and after heat treatment or grinding the surface is cleaned and re-examined.

Choosing between PT, MT and UT for oilfield parts

Method selection for typical oilfield items
PartPreferred methodReason
Overlay in a wellhead ring groovePTNon-magnetic alloy; flaws are surface-breaking
Drill collar thread rootMTFerromagnetic; fluorescent suspension is more sensitive
Stainless injection tubing weldPTSmall bore; non-magnetic
Wall of a treater shellUTPT shows no wall data
Embedded flaw in a forged bodyUTSurface methods cannot reach it

What the report contains

  • Customer, location, lease or rig, equipment tag and serial number.
  • Material, size and the standard or customer specification in force.
  • Procedure number, revision and the code edition behind it.
  • Penetrant, cleaner and developer with lot numbers, and certification of low halogen and sulfur content for alloys.
  • Surface temperature, dwell and developing times, and lighting level at inspection.
  • Indications with type, location, length and orientation, with a photograph or sketch.
  • Examiner, qualification level and report reviewer, plus areas not examined.
  • Acceptance wording only where the customer provides criteria.

What to send for a quote

  1. Parts list with material, size and quantity, and which items are installed or in a shop.
  2. Specification or code and its acceptance criteria.
  3. Overlay or alloy details, so we select compatible materials.
  4. Surface condition, cleaning responsibility and temperature.
  5. Site address, hazards such as H2S, and orientation steps.
  6. Report format and tagging convention.

Planning for oilfield schedules

Schedules move with rigs, repair shops and wellhead change-outs. We ask when parts will be cleaned and accessible, and mobilize accordingly. On wells with sour gas, site safety rules govern when and where the work is done. Winter in Colorado, the northern plains and Alaska demands enclosure and warmed materials, and hot summer surfaces in Texas and Kern County need shading. Solvent cleaners and developers are flammable, so permits and ignition-source controls apply near wells and production equipment.

Where we work in the United States

  • Midland: Permian wellhead repair shops, produced-water systems and sour facilities.
  • Bakersfield: Kern County heavy-oil and steam facilities under CalGEM oversight.
  • Oklahoma City: wellhead and pressure-control equipment suppliers.
  • Shreveport: Haynesville high-pressure trees and alloy tubing.
  • Denver: DJ Basin production and cold-weather planning.
  • San Antonio: Eagle Ford wellhead and completion hardware.
  • Tulsa: equipment manufacturers and fabricators in the mid-continent.
  • Anchorage: Alaska facilities where cold enclosures are required.
  • Houston: wellhead manufacturers, valve shops and service companies.

What we do not do

Industrial radiography in the United States is licensed under NRC or Agreement State rules and we do not perform it. We do not run drill-stem inspection lines, we do not calculate remaining life or fitness for service, and we do not offer crack sizing on this page. For the broader scope see weld inspection and MT versus PT compared.

Training your own technicians

Service companies and operators can develop their own penetrant technicians through PT Level 1 training and PT Level 2 training, with the penetrant testing simulator and oil and gas NDT training. The employer issues the certificate, and we help write the practice.

faq.q: What oilfield parts need penetrant instead of magnetic particle testing?
faq.a: Parts made of stainless steel, duplex, nickel alloy, aluminum or bronze, and weld overlay in wellhead ring grooves, because they do not respond to a magnetic field. Penetrant shows any crack open to the surface on these materials.

faq.q: Can penetrant testing find hidden cracks?
faq.a: No. It shows only flaws that are open to the surface. Embedded flaws and wall loss need ultrasonic testing, and we can pair methods on the same part.

faq.q: Which API documents apply to wellhead components?
faq.a: API Specification 6A governs wellhead and tree equipment, including overlay and surface examination expectations. The penetrant method follows ASME Section V, Article 6 and ASTM E165, and the customer’s specification sets acceptance.

faq.q: How do you prevent penetrant from damaging stainless parts?
faq.a: We use low-halogen and low-sulfur materials with certification, record lot numbers and remove residue after the test. Carbon-steel tools and brushes are kept away from stainless surfaces to avoid iron contamination.

faq.q: What temperatures can you test in?
faq.a: The standard surface range is roughly 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit unless the procedure is qualified for another range. Cold sites use heated enclosures, and hot surfaces are shaded or cooled before testing.

faq.q: Why does cleaning matter so much?
faq.a: Sludge, wax, paint, thread compound and smeared metal block the opening of a crack so penetrant cannot enter. Without proper cleaning and drying, a cracked part can appear sound.

faq.q: Who accepts or rejects penetrant indications?
faq.a: The equipment owner or its engineer does, applying the specification it names. We report indication type, location and size, plus non-relevant indications and why they were classified that way.

faq.q: What do you need from us to quote?
faq.a: The parts list with material, size and quantity, the specification and acceptance criteria, alloy details, surface condition and temperature, site address, hazards and orientation steps, and the report format.

faq.q: Do you inspect wellhead overlay in ring grooves?
faq.a: Yes. We examine overlay on sealing surfaces and ring grooves after the part is cleaned, using the owner’s procedure and reporting cracks and porosity; the owner decides on repair or retirement.
